title: Where do you cut the world?
hook: Tokyo and Los Angeles sit at opposite ends of most world maps. Are they really that far?

knows: that world maps usually have the Atlantic in the middle
longitude in degrees east and west of Greenwich
doesNotKnow: that a flat map must be cut somewhere
that the cut puts the Pacific's two sides at opposite edges

misconception: Distances between places on a world map are simply what they are; where the map is cut is neutral.
objective: The learner can explain that a world map must be cut somewhere, that the cut decides which places look far apart, and that Tokyo and Los Angeles are about 102° of map width apart on a Pacific-centred map versus 258° on a Greenwich-centred one.

claims.text: On a Greenwich-centred world map Tokyo and Los Angeles are about 258° of map width apart; on a map centred on 180° they are about 102° apart, about 2.5 times closer.
claims.source: Haneda 139.78°E and LAX 118.41°W differ by 258.19° of longitude; 360 - 258.19 = 101.81°; ratio 2.54 (shown as 2.5). Demo.tsx measures both from the projected x positions on its own Equirectangular map (gapDegrees). Coordinates of Haneda (35.55°N, 139.78°E) and LAX (33.94°N, 118.41°W) from memory of the airports' published reference points, not checked online. The brief used downtown LA (118.24°W) with Haneda; the lesson uses LAX for both ends being airports (258.0 vs 258.2, same rounding).

claims.text: On an Equirectangular map each degree of longitude is equally wide.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, Equidistant Cylindrical: x = R (λ - λ0). d3-geo geoEquirectangular. From memory, not checked online.

claims.text: The great-circle distance between Tokyo (Haneda) and Los Angeles (LAX) is about 8,810 km, and re-centring the map does not change it.
claims.source: d3-geo geoDistance x 6,371.0088 km on the coordinates in c1 = 8,812.6 km (shown rounded to 8,810). Sphere model. The slider only rotates the projection.

claims.text: Most world maps are cut so the Pacific's two sides sit at opposite edges; Greenwich in the middle is a convention, not a rule.
claims.source: Hook and reveal. Prime meridian adopted at the International Meridian Conference, 1884 (from memory). Pacific-centred world maps are standard in, for example, Chinese, Japanese and Australian atlases (from memory, not checked; the brief asks for two atlases to be cited as examples). Needs a source.

recall.question: Two cities look almost a full map-width apart on a world map. What does that tell you about the real distance between them?
options: They must be very far apart
Nothing by itself: they may be neighbours across the map's cut
They are on opposite sides of the Earth
recall.why: A flat map is cut somewhere. Places on either side of the cut appear at opposite edges even when they are close across it.
